adverse

/ad-VURS/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Adverse means antagonistic, unfavorable, or dangerous — working against you, often describing conditions, effects, or circumstances.

The new medication was pulled from trials after several patients reported adverse side effects, including dizziness and rashes.

Example

The airline delayed our flight for six hours, citing adverse weather conditions along the entire route.

The weather was actively working against a safe flight — unfavorable and potentially dangerous. Conditions that oppose your plans like this are adverse conditions.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unfavorable: Unfavorable conditions simply fail to help you — the odds, the weather, the timing are not on your side. Adverse is stronger: adverse conditions actively work against you, doing real harm rather than merely withholding help. An unfavorable review disappoints; an adverse reaction sends you to the doctor.

harmful: Harmful means causing damage or hurt, and it points at the damage itself — harmful chemicals, harmful habits. Adverse points at the direction of the force: adverse conditions or effects are set against your success, whether or not the damage has landed yet. Harmful reports the wound; adverse reports the opposition.

hostile: Hostile means aggressively working against you, with the flavor of an enemy's intent — hostile troops, a hostile crowd, a hostile takeover. Adverse opposition has no actor and no intent behind it: storms, side effects, and market swings are adverse. If it feels like an attack, it is hostile; if it is simply against you, it is adverse.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

favorable: helping things go well

beneficial: producing good results

Where it sits · how actively it harms you

unhelpful → adverse → disastrous

unhelpful vs. adverse: Unhelpful conditions merely fail to assist you; adverse conditions actively work against you.

disastrous vs. adverse: Adverse effects cause real harm; disastrous effects cause complete ruin.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ad-: toward — here, turned toward as an opponent (Latin)

Root — -verse: turned (Latin vertere/versus, "to turn")

Put it together: Adverse literally means "turned toward you" as an opponent — adverse conditions are circumstances that have turned to face you and stand in your way.

Use the root in a new word: reverse: She threw the car into reverse and backed slowly out of the narrow driveway.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal — medical, legal & scientific

Watch out for the classic trap: adverse is not the same word as averse. Adverse describes things — conditions, effects, reactions, circumstances — that work against you. Averse (a completely different word) describes a person who is reluctant or opposed to something. A simple rule: conditions are adverse; people are averse.
